Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The failing test `testMissedEndEvent()` concerns integration using the DormandPrince853Integrator over a short time interval. The failure is that integration goes significantly past the specified end time, violating the expected end boundary. According to the bug report, this problem stems from the integrator treating the end of the integration range as an event. Numerical errors in event detection cause imprecise event location, allowing the integrator to advance beyond the final target time, sometimes by a large margin (e.g., intending to integrate over 60 seconds, but actually integrating over 160 seconds).

The DormandPrince853Integrator extends an adaptive stepsize integrator which controls step sizes between a minimum and maximum step. It has mechanisms (such as `filterStep`) for bounding step sizes, but more importantly it uses event handlers to detect when integration reaches specified events, including the end time. The essential problem is the accuracy and reliability of event detection near the integration boundary.

The integrator presumably uses a root-finding algorithm or event locating procedure to find when the event occurs and to stop integration at that point. The test demonstrates that the event (final time) is not properly located, so integration proceeds beyond it.

The test sets initial time, final time, initial step size, and integrates a simple ODE with small state and derivative values, aiming for very tight tolerances (1e-10). Despite this, the integrator overshoots the final time.

Since the DormandPrince853Integrator inherits the event handling and step filtering features from its superclass (adaptive stepsize integrator class), the root cause is likely related to insufficient precision or robustness in either the event location logic or the step adjustment when approaching the final time event.

The recent bug reports do not mention anything relevant about event handling or integration beyond bounds.

In summary, the bug is caused by improper or imprecise event location for the final integration boundary event, resulting in integration passing beyond the specified end time.

Next step: Identify methods managing event location and step acceptance near the end time in DormandPrince853Integrator or its superclass AdaptiveStepsizeIntegrator, especially methods responsible for checking and enforcing end time stopping conditions and event detection. Relevant methods include the integration method itself, step acceptance handlers, and event location/root finding.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
